pages.title: Kitchens
pages.content:
KITCHENS

EIGHT COUNTERS · ONE ROOF

Eight counters, one roof

Eight independent kitchens cook under one roof at Hiroba Food Hall, each dedicated to a single culinary craft. From morning broth to afternoon filter coffee, every counter prepares lunch to order for the shared tables.

The Eight Kitchen Counters

Ladle Lane is led by Tomás Ferreira, preparing clear chicken noodle soup, sesame broth with greens, and cold noodles with herbs. At Ember Grill, Amara Osei grills over charcoal, serving flatbread with grilled squash, chicken skewer plates, and yoghurt and herb dip. Green Counter is guided by Lena Kowalski, focusing on barley bowls, roast roots and lentils, and fresh seasonal leaves. Daniel Cho runs Wok Row, tossing egg fried rice, charred greens, and seasoned pepper tofu over high flames. Spice Shelf brings slow-simmered curries from Priya Nair, including lentil dal, chickpea and spinach curry, and seasoned rice with pickles. Marco Bellini leads Fresca with handmade pasta, offering tagliatelle with tomato, ricotta ravioli, and bean and pasta soup. Ingrid Holm bakes daily at Bakehouse, preparing fresh soup and rye bread, cheese toasties, and warm cardamom buns. Finally, Steep is managed by the hall team under Ruth Adeyemi, serving filter coffee, black tea, and almond cake.

Kitchen Service Hours and Ordering

Most kitchens at Hiroba Food Hall operate Monday through Friday from 11:00 to 15:00 for lunch and 17:00 to 21:30 for dinner, as well as Saturday from 12:00 to 21:30. Steep and Bakehouse operate continuously from 11:00 until closing at 17:00. Guests order directly at each counter rail. You can choose a single lunch plate for €12.50 or order a two-kitchen tray for €14.00, combining half portions from two different counters on one wooden tray. Full pricing details for bowls, soups, and group sets are listed on our dedicated prices page.

pages.title: Lunch Hour
pages.content:
LUNCH HOUR

THE DAY, STAMP BY STAMP

The hall, hour by hour

Weekday lunch at Hiroba Food Hall runs from 11:00 to 15:00, structured around the midday rhythm of the city. Kitchens cook to order while long shared tables keep seating fluid and unhurried.

The Midday Rhythm from Eleven to Three

At 11:00, doors open as wooden trays, water carafes, and cutlery are set along the rail. By 11:45, early tables begin to fill, and kitchens fire their first bowls of broth and pasta. The midday peak arrives at 12:10, when guests with held tables are seated first and queues form independently across the eight counters. At 13:00, the second wave takes their places as tables turn and filter coffee starts pouring steadily at Steep. The final lunch orders are taken at 14:30, giving slow eaters quiet time before the hall resets at 15:00. Evening service resumes when dinner kitchens open at 17:00, running until the last tables finish at 21:30.

Pacing the Peak: Trays, Rails, and Kitchen Lines

Hiroba Food Hall is deliberately paced so that lunch moves smoothly even during the peak between 12:10 and 13:00. Guests pick up a tray and cutlery at the entrance rail before choosing where to order. Because ordering happens separately at each individual kitchen counter, lines rarely bunch into a single bottleneck. Colleagues can split up across different stations—ordering noodles, skewers, salads, or curry—and rejoin each other without delay. Reserved places are marked with a simple wooden block, so held tables are seated immediately without waiting in arrival lines. Clear table turnover and dedicated tray return stations ensure shared tables remain clean and available throughout the hour.

How do you book and hold a lunch table?

When you arrive at the hall, your designated seating area along the long shared tables will be marked with a small wooden block. We keep every held table for exactly fifteen minutes past your booked time before releasing it to walking guests. Holding a table is entirely free of charge, ensuring your party can sit together without stress.

What are the group policies and accessibility arrangements?

pages.title: Prices
pages.content:
PRICES

SEVEN LUNCH PRICES

One price list for every kitchen

All eight kitchens share a clear, transparent pricing structure across weekday lunch and evening service. Prices are fixed in euros, and holding a table never costs anything.

What are the lunch prices across the hall?

Every kitchen at Hiroba Food Hall works to a unified price schedule. A standard lunch plate containing one main dish and one side from any kitchen costs €12.50. Dedicated noodle or curry bowls are priced at €11.00, while a grain bowl is €10.50. For those wishing to taste from multiple counters, the two-kitchen tray offers half portions from two separate kitchens on one wooden tray for €14.00. A nourishing bowl of soup with freshly baked bread is €8.00, and hot filter coffee or black tea is €3.00. For gatherings of six to twelve guests booked 24 hours in advance, the group lunch set is €18.00 per person. Holding a table is always free.

How do kitchens handle dietary requirements and allergens?

Because each kitchen prepares dishes fresh from scratch, ingredient transparency is straightforward. All eight counters clearly document and display the 14 EU allergens on their daily boards. Whether you avoid gluten, dairy, nuts, or shellfish, you can speak directly with the kitchen leads and cooks at the counter before placing your order. Plant-based and vegetarian options are readily available at Green Counter, Spice Shelf, Ladle Lane, and Bakehouse. If you are ordering a two-kitchen tray or coordinating meals for a group set, staff at both counters will gladly verify ingredients to ensure your selections remain safe and properly separated.

pages.title: About the Hall
pages.content:
THE HALL

SINCE 2019

A hall built around one lunch hour

Founded in 2019, Hiroba Food Hall brings eight independent kitchens together under the roof of a former Rotterdam harbour warehouse. We built this space around shared tables and the rhythm of weekday lunch.

A Harbour Warehouse Built for Shared Dining

Hiroba Food Hall opened on 4 March 2019 on the ground floor of a converted harbour warehouse at Havenhof 12 in Rotterdam. The building was designed to offer an open, communal alternative to conventional city dining. Inside, 180 seats are arranged along broad wooden shared tables, complemented by a 24-stool counter facing the open kitchens. Natural daylight pours in through high warehouse windows, illuminating a busy dining room where office workers, neighbours, and visitors sit shoulder to shoulder.

Eight Independent Kitchens on One Tray

We chose eight distinct kitchens so each culinary team could concentrate deeply on a single craft instead of trying to cook everything. Each counter operates autonomously, from handmade pasta and slow curries to charcoal skewers and stone-ground grains. Yet dining remains unified. Guests collect one wooden tray, order whatever combination of dishes they prefer, and sit together at the same table without compromising anyone's taste. The two-kitchen tray embodies this philosophy, letting diners pair half portions from two different counters on a single tray for €14.00. It turns lunch into an effortless shared exploration across culinary traditions.

Why Weekday Lunch is the Heart of the Hall

As hall manager since our opening in 2019, Ruth Adeyemi views weekday lunch as the anchor of Hiroba Food Hall. Between 11:00 and 15:00, the hall becomes the dining room for Rotterdam's working day. When the peak hits at 12:10, our pacing keeps the energy vibrant rather than chaotic. Tables turn smoothly, held spots are respected, and guests can take forty minutes away from their desks to enjoy honest food cooked right before their eyes. When three o'clock comes, the hall resets quietly, wiping down tables and refreshing the floor before evening service begins again at five.

We set the pace of the room around 12:10. Everything else follows from that.

Ruth Adeyemi, hall manager since 2019

pages.title: People
pages.content:
PEOPLE

EIGHT LEADS · ONE HALL

The people behind the counters

Eight dedicated culinary leads direct the kitchens and hospitality of Hiroba Food Hall. Each craftsperson brings a distinct discipline, shaping the character of our shared counters.

TF

Tomás Ferreira

Lead, Ladle Lane

Brings quiet precision to simmered broths and noodle dishes. He is at the pot long before the doors open.

AO

Amara Osei

Lead, Ember Grill

Manages the open charcoal hearth, turning chicken skewers and baking flatbreads over glowing embers.

LK

Lena Kowalski

Lead, Green Counter

Curates wholesome grain bowls layered with barley, roast roots, lentils and seasonal leaves.

Lead, Wok Row

Applies intense wok heat to egg fried rice, charred greens and flash-seared pepper tofu.

Lead, Spice Shelf

Stews lentil dal and chickpea and spinach curry, served with fragrant rice and house pickles.

MB

Marco Bellini

Lead, Fresca

Rolls and cuts fresh pasta every morning: tagliatelle, ricotta ravioli and bean and pasta soup.

IH

Ingrid Holm

Lead, Bakehouse

Handles the daily baking: rye bread, cheese toasties and warm cardamom buns.

RA

Ruth Adeyemi

Hall manager since 2019, Steep

Looks after hospitality and table holds, and runs Steep: filter coffee, black tea and almond cake.

The Savoury and Hearth Kitchen Leads

Tomás Ferreira heads Ladle Lane, bringing quiet precision to simmered broths and noodle dishes that warm the midday crowd. At Ember Grill, Amara Osei manages the open charcoal hearth, turning seasoned chicken skewers and baking fresh flatbreads over glowing embers. Daniel Cho commands Wok Row, applying intense wok heat to crisp vegetables, fried rice, and flash-seared pepper tofu in rapid rhythm. Over at Fresca, Marco Bellini rolls and cuts fresh pasta every morning, serving rich tagliatelle, delicate ricotta ravioli, and hearty bean soups that reflect traditional Italian bench work.

Grains, Spices, Bakery, and Hall Hospitality

Lena Kowalski curates Green Counter, assembling wholesome grain bowls layered with barley, roasted root vegetables, lentils, and seasonal greens. Priya Nair leads Spice Shelf, stewing aromatic lentil dals and chickpea spinach curries paired with fragrant rice and tangy house pickles. At Bakehouse, Ingrid Holm handles daily baking, producing hearty rye breads, golden cheese toasties, and fragrant cardamom buns. Steering overall operations and running Steep is Ruth Adeyemi, hall manager since 2019. Ruth looks after hospitality, table reservations, and our specialty filter coffee, tea, and almond cakes.

pages.title: Visit the Hall
pages.content:
VISIT

HAVENHOF 12 · ROTTERDAM

Find the hall at Havenhof

Located at Havenhof 12 in Rotterdam, Hiroba Food Hall welcomes diners Monday through Saturday in a converted harbour warehouse. Step inside for lunch or dinner, or find a quiet counter stool between services.

Hiroba Food Hall, Havenhof 12, 3011 AB Rotterdam, Netherlands

Hours

Mon–Fri 11:00–21:30

Sat 12:00–21:30

What are the hall opening hours and service times?

Hiroba Food Hall is open Monday through Friday from 11:00 to 21:30 and Saturday from 12:00 to 21:30. We are closed on Sundays. Weekday lunch service runs from 11:00 to 15:00, with last lunch orders placed at 14:30 before our afternoon reset. Between 15:00 and 17:00, the main hall remains quiet while Steep and Bakehouse serve warm drinks, tea, and buns until 17:00. Evening kitchens open at 17:00 and serve dinner until closing. Seating is spacious and open, offering 180 seats across communal tables and 24 counter stools.

How do you reach Havenhof and where can you park?

Our warehouse is situated at Havenhof 12, 3011 AB Rotterdam. Arriving by public transit is easy: take Tram 8 directly to the Havenhof stop, which leaves you just a 4-minute walk from our front entrance. Cyclists will find 60 dedicated bicycle racks installed right outside the front doors. Please be aware that there is no customer car park on site, so we strongly encourage arriving by public transport, bicycle, or on foot. The hall entrance is completely step-free, and six accessible lower tables are positioned near the entrance for guests with limited mobility.

pages.title: Contact
pages.content:
CONTACT

WRITE TO THE HALL

Write to the hall, and we answer

Get in touch with the team at Hiroba Food Hall to hold a table, enquire about group lunches, or ask questions about our kitchens. Ruth Adeyemi and our hall team respond promptly.

Email hello@hiroba-hall.example

Phone +31 10 555 0190

Address Hiroba Food Hall, Havenhof 12, 3011 AB Rotterdam, Netherlands

Hours

Mon–Fri 11:00–21:30

Sat 12:00–21:30

How can you get in touch with our hall team?

You can reach the Hiroba Food Hall management desk directly by email at hello@hiroba-hall.example or by telephone at +31 10 555 0190. We are located at Havenhof 12, 3011 AB Rotterdam, Netherlands. Our doors are open Monday through Friday from 11:00 to 21:30 and Saturday from 12:00 to 21:30, with weekday lunch running between 11:00 and 15:00 and last lunch orders at 14:30. Whether you have questions regarding kitchen menus, lost property, or allergen protocols, hall manager Ruth Adeyemi and our hosting team are here to assist you.

How do group lunch enquiries and table holdings work?

Holding a table at Hiroba Food Hall is free and straightforward. Tables can be reserved for groups of two to twelve diners. For casual weekday lunch visits, message or call us by 11:00 on the day; your table will be identified with a wooden block and held for fifteen minutes past your booking time. Parties of six to twelve guests are asked to book at least 24 hours in advance to secure places together and arrange our group lunch set at €18.00 per person. Please mention if your party requires any of our six step-free lower tables.

Ruth Adeyemi
Hall manager, Hiroba Food Hall

posts.title: A table for twelve on a Thursday
posts.excerpt: How twelve colleagues navigated the midday lunch peak at Hiroba Food Hall with a held table and plates from across eight kitchens.
posts.content:
At eleven o'clock on Wednesday morning, twenty-four hours before their planned lunch, an office coordinator from a studio down Havenhof sent a short note to hello@hiroba-hall.example. The request was straightforward: a table for twelve colleagues arriving together at 12:10 on Thursday afternoon. Group bookings of six to twelve guests require twenty-four hours of notice at Hiroba Food Hall, giving Ruth Adeyemi and the hall team time to allocate a continuous stretch along the long shared wooden tables. Within half an hour, confirmation arrived. When Thursday noon approached, the table near the tall harbour windows was set aside with a small wooden block marker, waiting quietly as the dining room began to fill.

Walking into the converted harbour warehouse at Havenhof 12 just as the clock struck 12:10, the group found the hall entering its peak midday rush. On ordinary days, finding twelve adjacent seats during the peak between 12:10 and 13:00 would challenge any party in the city. Here, the held table policy provided an effortless anchor. Hiroba keeps held tables for fifteen minutes past the reserved arrival time, requiring no deposit and carrying no booking fee. The party bypassed the arrival hesitation entirely, setting coats down at their marked table before heading back to the tray rail to collect wooden trays, cutlery, and water carafes.

The true beauty of dining with twelve people under one roof is that no one compromises on their appetite. Because the hall houses eight independent kitchens rather than a single compromised menu, the party scattered across the floor in pairs and trios. Two colleagues lined up at Ladle Lane, where Tomás Ferreira was lifting noodles from simmering broth pots for clear chicken soup and sesame bowls. Another walked toward Ember Grill, drawn by the scent of charcoal as Amara Osei turned seasoned chicken skewers and charred flatbreads. Across the hall, plates of fresh ricotta ravioli from Marco Bellini at Fresca joined barley bowls from Lena Kowalski at Green Counter and lentil dal from Priya Nair at Spice Shelf.

Ordering was swift because each counter maintains its own independent line. Instead of a single queue stretching toward the door, orders moved concurrently across all eight stations. For groups choosing our group lunch set at €18.00 per person, coordinating meal selections across multiple counters is completely seamless. Several diners opted for the two-kitchen tray, bringing half portions of charred greens from Daniel Cho at Wok Row alongside warm soup and rye bread from Ingrid Holm at Bakehouse. Within ten minutes of reaching the counters, all twelve trays had returned to the table, filled with varied ceramic bowls and plates.

Eating together at long shared tables brings a distinct sense of occasion without the stiffness of formal reservations. For forty minutes, the colleagues traded skewer bites, shared bowls of yoghurt herb dip, and caught up on project work against the gentle hum of the hall. Around them, the dining room functioned at full capacity, with all 180 seats and 24 counter stools occupied by workers from across Rotterdam. Yet because the hall is paced so deliberately, the atmosphere remained calm and conversational.

By 13:00, as the second midday wave began to arrive, lunch was winding down. Ruth Adeyemi and the hall team began pouring filter coffee and black tea at Steep, sending plates of almond cake across the counter to round off the meal. The twelve colleagues stacked their wooden trays at the return rail, stepped out through the step-free entrance, and walked back into Havenhof before the half-past-one rush. It was another ordinary Thursday at the hall: eight kitchens cooking to order, one table held without fuss, and twelve people fed well within the hour.

posts.title: Two kitchens on one tray
posts.excerpt: The two-kitchen tray: half portions from two counters, carried to the table together.
posts.content:
The two-kitchen tray is the hall’s quietest idea. You take half a portion from one kitchen and half from another, and they travel on a single tray for €14.00.

A favourite pairs a small bowl of clear chicken noodle soup from Ladle Lane with flatbread and yoghurt dip from Ember Grill. The cooks at the pass keep the portions even.

Ask at either counter; there is nothing to book.

posts.title: What 12:10 looks like from the pass
posts.excerpt: Tomás Ferreira on the minutes when the queue turns and the first big wave arrives.
posts.content:
At 12:10 the first big wave reaches Ladle Lane. Tomás Ferreira has been at the pot since early morning and by now the broth is exactly where he wants it.

“You stop looking at the queue and start looking at the tickets,” he says. Held tables are seated first, the queue moves by kitchen, and the rail keeps trays flowing.

By 13:00 the second wave comes in, tables turn and coffee starts at Steep.

posts.title: Why the hall resets at three
posts.excerpt: Ruth Adeyemi on the afternoon pause between lunch and the evening kitchens.
posts.content:
After the last lunch order at 14:30 the hall quietens for slow eaters. At 15:00 the tables are wiped, the rail is cleared and the cooks take a breath.

Ruth Adeyemi, hall manager since 2019, calls it the hall’s second breakfast: a short reset before the evening kitchens open at 17:00.

Coffee and tea from Steep are served through the afternoon.
